title: hashcat
description: Hashcat is a GPU-accelerated password recovery tool supporting hundreds of hash types via OpenCL/CUDA/Metal backends, with dictionary, mask, combinator, and hybrid attack modes.

Getting Started.Getting Started:
Current stable release is **hashcat 7.1.2** (Aug 2025), which added a Metal backend for Apple GPUs alongside the existing OpenCL/CUDA/HIP backends. On Arch Linux it's packaged as `hashcat`.

## 1. Install

```bash
sudo pacman -S hashcat
```

For NVIDIA GPU acceleration you also need the proprietary driver and OpenCL runtime:

```bash
sudo pacman -S nvidia opencl-nvidia
```

For AMD:

```bash
sudo pacman -S rocm-opencl-runtime
```

## 2. Verify backends

```bash
hashcat -I
```

Lists every detected compute device (CPU and GPU) and which backend (OpenCL/CUDA/HIP) can drive it. If your GPU is missing, the runtime package above usually isn't installed correctly.

## 3. Benchmark

```bash
hashcat -b -m 0
```

Runs the built-in benchmark for hash mode `0` (raw MD5) so you can sanity-check GPU throughput before a real job.

## ⚠️ Authorization notice

Only crack hashes you own or are explicitly authorized to test. See [Legal Notes](/hashcat/legal-notes/).
Getting Started.Attack Modes:
Hashcat's `-a` flag selects the attack mode — the strategy for generating candidate passwords, independent of the hash type (`-m`).

| Mode | `-a` | Description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Straight | `0` | One wordlist, optionally with `-r` rules |
| Combinator | `1` | Concatenates words from two wordlists |
| Brute-force / mask | `3` | Character-set mask, e.g. `?u?l?l?l?l?d?d` |
| Hybrid wordlist+mask | `6` | Wordlist entry + appended mask |
| Hybrid mask+wordlist | `7` | Mask + appended wordlist entry |
| Association | `9` | Candidate tied to a specific hash (e.g. cracking a KeePass entry using its own username) |

## Straight mode with rules

```bash
hashcat -m 0 -a 0 hashes.txt rockyou.txt -r rules/best64.rule
```

## Mask mode

```bash
hashcat -m 0 -a 3 hashes.txt ?u?l?l?l?l?l?d?d
```

Mask charsets: `?l` lowercase, `?u` uppercase, `?d` digit, `?s` symbol, `?a` all printable, `?b` any byte.

## Hybrid mode

```bash
hashcat -m 0 -a 6 hashes.txt rockyou.txt ?d?d?d?d
```

Every wordlist word gets a 4-digit suffix tried against it — covers `password2024`-style patterns a plain wordlist misses.
Getting Started.Hash Modes:
`-m` selects the hash algorithm/format. There are 300+ modes; a few commonly needed ones:

| Mode | Hash type |
| --- | --- |
| `0` | Raw MD5 |
| `100` | Raw SHA1 |
| `1000` | NTLM |
| `1800` | sha512crypt (`$6$`, modern Linux `/etc/shadow`) |
| `3200` | bcrypt |
| `1400` | Raw SHA256 |
| `22000` | WPA-PBKDF2-PMKID+EAPOL (modern Wi-Fi handshake format) |
| `13100` | Kerberos 5 TGS-REP etype 23 |

## Finding the right mode

```bash
hashcat --identify hashes.txt
```

Guesses likely `-m` values from the hash's structure — a good first step when you're not sure what you're looking at.

```bash
hashcat --help | grep -i bcrypt
```

Or grep the full mode list for a keyword to find the exact numeric mode.
Getting Started.Legal Notes:
Hashcat is a password-recovery and security-auditing tool. Cracking a hash you don't have explicit authorization to test — including hashes belonging to someone else's accounts, or extracted during unauthorized access — is illegal under computer-crime statutes in most jurisdictions, regardless of how the hash was obtained.

Legitimate uses include: auditing your own organization's password policy strength (with authorization), recovering a password you've forgotten for your own account/file, and authorized penetration testing engagements with signed scope.

Guides.Cracking Wifi Handshakes:
## Capture a handshake

Use a wireless tool (e.g. `airodump-ng` from the `aircrack-ng` suite) to capture a WPA handshake or PMKID, then convert it to hashcat's `.hc22000` format with `hcxpcapngtool` (from the `hcxtools` package):

```bash
sudo pacman -S hcxtools
hcxpcapngtool -o hash.hc22000 capture.pcapng
```

## Crack it

```bash
hashcat -m 22000 -a 0 hash.hc22000 rockyou.txt
```

Only attempt this against a network you own or are authorized to audit.

## Show the recovered key

```bash
hashcat -m 22000 --show hash.hc22000
```
Guides.Rule Based Attacks:
Rules mutate each wordlist candidate — the single biggest lever for cracking human-chosen passwords without an astronomically large wordlist.

## Built-in rule files

Hashcat ships several under `/usr/share/hashcat/rules/` (path may vary by distro packaging):

| Rule file | Style |
| --- | --- |
| `best64.rule` | Small, high-yield rule set — good default |
| `d3ad0ne.rule` | Larger, broader coverage |
| `rockyou-30000.rule` | Rules mined from real cracked password patterns |

```bash
hashcat -m 1000 -a 0 hashes.txt rockyou.txt -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule
```

## Chaining multiple rule files

```bash
hashcat -m 1000 -a 0 hashes.txt rockyou.txt \
  -r best64.rule -r toggles1.rule
```

Each candidate gets every combination of rules from both files applied — this multiplies keyspace quickly, so watch runtime on large wordlists.

*Part of the [Attack Modes](/hashcat/attack-modes/) page.* Hand off from John the Ripper's hash-extraction scripts straight into a hashcat GPU run.

Source: `example/john_to_hashcat.sh`

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

ZIP="${1:?usage: john_to_hashcat.sh <file.zip>}"

zip2john "$ZIP" > /tmp/zip.hash
hashcat -m 13600 -a 0 /tmp/zip.hash \
  /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt \
  -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule
hashcat -m 13600 --show /tmp/zip.hash
```

Run it:

```bash
chmod +x example/john_to_hashcat.sh
./example/john_to_hashcat.sh secrets.zip
```
Guides.Custom Charsets And Increment Mode:
## Custom charsets

```bash
hashcat -m 0 -a 3 hashes.txt -1 '?l?u' '?1?1?1?1?d?d' hashes.txt
```

`-1` through `-4` define up to four custom placeholder classes for mask mode; `?1` in the mask then means "one character from whichever set `-1` defines" (here, either case of a letter). Handy when the built-in `?a` (all printable) is far broader than the actual password policy you're targeting.

## Increment mode: trying every length automatically

```bash
hashcat -m 0 -a 3 --increment --increment-min=4 --increment-max=8 \
  hashes.txt ?a?a?a?a?a?a?a?a
```

Without `--increment`, a mask of eight `?a`s tries *only* 8-character candidates. `--increment` instead tries every length from `--increment-min` up to the mask's own length (here, 4 through 8) — essential when you don't know the exact password length, since a mask alone commits to one fixed length.

## Hex charsets, for non-ASCII or awkward characters

```bash
hashcat -m 0 -a 3 --hex-charset -1 4142434445 hashes.txt ?1?1?1?1
```

`--hex-charset` reads custom charset definitions as hex byte pairs instead of literal characters — useful for including bytes that are awkward to pass safely on a command line (quotes, backslashes, non-printable bytes).
Guides.Sessions, Potfile, And Resuming:
Long-running jobs need to survive reboots, interruptions, and repeated attempts without wasting GPU time on hashes already solved.

## Naming and resuming a session

```bash
hashcat -m 1000 -a 0 hashes.txt rockyou.txt --session=ntlm_audit
```

```bash
hashcat --session=ntlm_audit --restore
```

`--session=NAME` writes periodic checkpoint state; `--restore` (with the same session name, or omitted to restore the most recent) picks a run back up from where it stopped, whether that was `Ctrl+C`, a crash, or a reboot.

## Live status while it runs

```bash
hashcat -m 1000 -a 0 hashes.txt rockyou.txt --status --status-timer=10
```

`--status` turns on automatic periodic status lines (speed, progress %, ETA) instead of only updating when you press a key; `--status-timer` sets how often, in seconds.

## The potfile

Cracked results are written to `~/.local/share/hashcat/hashcat.potfile` by default, so re-running the same job never re-attacks an already-solved hash — it just reports the cached result instantly.

```bash
hashcat --potfile-path=./audit.potfile -m 1000 hashes.txt rockyou.txt
hashcat --potfile-disable -m 1000 hashes.txt rockyou.txt
```

`--potfile-path` keeps separate engagements' results from mixing; `--potfile-disable` skips the potfile entirely (e.g. for a quick one-off test you don't want cached).

## Removing cracked hashes from the input as you go

```bash
hashcat -m 1000 -a 0 hashes.txt rockyou.txt --remove --remove-timer=60
```

`--remove` rewrites the hash file, stripping out hashes as they're cracked, so a subsequent attack mode only spends time on what's left; `--remove-timer` controls how often (seconds) that rewrite happens during a long run.
Guides.Performance Tuning:
Getting the GPU actually saturated is often the difference between a job finishing overnight versus over a week.

## Workload profile

```bash
hashcat -m 0 -a 0 hashes.txt rockyou.txt -w 3
```

`-w` (`--workload-profile`) trades desktop responsiveness for throughput: `1` low, `2` default, `3` high, `4` "nightmare" (expect the GUI to stutter). `-w 3` is a common sweet spot on a dedicated cracking box; keep `-w 1`–`2` on a machine you're also using interactively.

## Kernel acceleration and loop tuning

```bash
hashcat -m 0 -a 0 hashes.txt rockyou.txt -n 80 -u 1024
```

`-n` (`--kernel-accel`) and `-u` (`--kernel-loops`) control how much work is batched per GPU kernel launch. Hashcat auto-tunes these reasonably well; manual tuning is mostly useful for squeezing out the last few percent on a well-understood, fixed hash type — leave them alone unless you have a specific benchmark showing a gain.

## Restricting or excluding backends/devices

```bash
hashcat -I
hashcat -m 0 -a 0 hashes.txt rockyou.txt -d 1
hashcat -m 0 -a 0 hashes.txt rockyou.txt --backend-ignore-cuda
```

`-d <ids>` (comma-separated, from the `-I` listing) restricts a run to specific devices — useful on a multi-GPU box to dedicate one GPU to hashcat while another renders a display. `--backend-ignore-cuda`/`--backend-ignore-opencl`/`--backend-ignore-hip` disable a whole backend, handy when a broken driver for one backend is slowing device detection down or causing spurious errors.

## Optimized kernels

```bash
hashcat -m 0 -a 0 hashes.txt rockyou.txt -O
```

`-O` (`--optimized-kernel-enable`) uses faster kernels with a password-length ceiling (usually 32 bytes, mode-dependent) — a large speed win, safe to always use unless you specifically expect passwords longer than the limit.

CLI Reference.hashcat:
## Synopsis

```
hashcat [options] hashfile [dictionary|mask|directory]
```

## Hash and attack selection

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-m <mode>` | Hash type (numeric mode) |
| `-a <mode>` | Attack mode: `0` straight, `1` combinator, `3` mask, `6`/`7` hybrid, `9` association |
| `--identify` | Guess likely `-m` values for the given hash file |
| `--username` | Input lines include a `user:hash` prefix to strip |
| `--hex-salt` / `--hex-wordlist` | Treat salt/wordlist entries as hex-encoded |

## Rules and masks

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-r <file>` | Rule file for straight/hybrid modes (repeatable) |
| `-j <rule>` / `-k <rule>` | Apply a single inline rule to the left/right dictionary (combinator mode) |
| `-1`..`-4 <charset>` | Custom charset for mask placeholders `?1`..`?4` |
| `--increment` | Try every candidate length, not just the mask's own length |
| `--increment-min` / `--increment-max` | Bound the lengths tried with `--increment` |
| `--hex-charset` | Read `-1`..`-4` charsets as hex byte pairs |

## Session, output, and resuming

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-o <file>` | Write cracked results to file |
| `--outfile-format=N` | Format of `-o` output (hash, plain, hex-plain, etc. — see `--help`) |
| `--show` | Show already-cracked hashes from the potfile |
| `--left` | Show hashes that were *not* cracked |
| `--session=NAME` | Name this run for later `--restore` |
| `--restore` | Resume the named/last interrupted session |
| `--potfile-path=FILE` | Use an alternate potfile |
| `--potfile-disable` | Don't read/write a potfile at all |
| `--remove` | Strip cracked hashes from the input file as they're found |
| `--remove-timer=SEC` | How often `--remove` rewrites the file |
| `--loopback` | After finishing, re-run using newly cracked passwords as a wordlist |

## Devices and performance

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-I` | List available compute devices |
| `-d <ids>` | Restrict to specific device IDs |
| `-w <1-4>` | Workload profile (`1`=low interference … `4`=nightmare) |
| `-O` | Enable optimized (length-limited) kernels |
| `-n <N>` | Kernel acceleration (manual tuning) |
| `-u <N>` | Kernel loops (manual tuning) |
| `--backend-ignore-cuda` / `-opencl` / `-hip` | Disable a whole compute backend |

## Status and diagnostics

| Option | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `-b`, `--benchmark` | Run benchmark mode |
| `--benchmark-all` | Benchmark every hash mode, not just common ones |
| `--status` | Enable automatic periodic status updates |
| `--status-timer=SEC` | Interval for `--status` updates |
| `--machine-readable` | Status output in a script-friendly format |
| `--speed-only` | Estimate speed only, without actually attacking |
| `--quiet` | Suppress non-essential output |
| `--force` | Bypass warnings (e.g. unsupported device) — use cautiously |
| `-V`, `--version` | Print version and exit |

Full option list: `hashcat --help`, or [hashcat.net/wiki](https://hashcat.net/wiki/) for the maintained reference.

Project.FAQ:
### `No devices found/left` at startup

Usually a missing or mismatched OpenCL/CUDA runtime. Run `hashcat -I` to see what's detected; if nothing appears, (re)install the vendor runtime package (`opencl-nvidia` or `rocm-opencl-runtime` on Arch) and confirm `clinfo` also sees the device.

### Cracking speed is much lower than expected benchmarks

Check the workload profile (`-w`) — the default is conservative to keep the desktop responsive. `-w 3` or `-w 4` push GPU utilization much higher at the cost of desktop responsiveness during the run.

### `Exhausted` with no crack, but I'm sure the password is in my wordlist

Check for encoding issues (the wordlist might not be UTF-8, or the hash expects a different encoding via `--encoding-from`), or confirm the correct `-m` mode — a wrong-but-similar mode number silently produces zero matches instead of an error.

### `--restore` says the session doesn't match

Restoring requires the exact same command-line options as the original run (same hash file, mode, attack mode, wordlist/mask) — hashcat checks this and refuses to resume with mismatched parameters, since the checkpoint only makes sense against the original keyspace.

### Should I use John the Ripper or hashcat?

They overlap a lot. Hashcat is GPU-first and typically far faster for GPU-friendly fast hashes (raw MD5/SHA1, NTLM) and has the most mature Wi-Fi handshake and rule-attack tooling. John (especially the jumbo build) supports more "unusual" formats out of the box and has richer built-in file-format extraction (`*2john` scripts) — many workflows use John to extract and identify a hash, then hand it to hashcat for the actual cracking, as shown in [Examples](/hashcat/examples/).

### `--loopback` didn't try anything new

`--loopback` only re-runs using passwords newly cracked *during this session* as a wordlist for a follow-up straight attack — if this run found nothing new, there's nothing for it to loop back with. It's typically added after a mask or rule attack, chaining "attack once, then extend with whatever it found" in one command.

Learn by Examples.Auditing Your Own Wi-Fi And A Forgotten:
Two authorized, personal tasks in one session: checking whether your own home Wi-Fi's WPA2 password is crackable with a common wordlist, and recovering a forgotten password on your own encrypted ZIP backup. Together these exercise most of hashcat's everyday workflow.

## 1. Check the hardware first

```bash
hashcat -I
hashcat -b -m 0
```

`-I` confirms a GPU is actually detected before committing to a long run; `-b -m 0` benchmarks raw MD5 as a quick sanity check of overall throughput.

## Part A: Wi-Fi handshake

## 2. Capture a handshake (own network only)

Using `airodump-ng` from the aircrack-ng suite on your own access point (see the [aircrack-ng docs](/aircrack-ng/)), save a capture, then convert it to hashcat's format:

```bash
sudo pacman -S hcxtools
hcxpcapngtool -o home_wifi.hc22000 capture.pcapng
```

## 3. Identify the mode (or just know it: 22000)

```bash
hashcat --identify home_wifi.hc22000
```

Confirms `22000` (WPA-PBKDF2-PMKID+EAPOL), the modern combined format that superseded the older separate `2500`/`16800` modes.

## 4. First pass: straight wordlist with rules

```bash
hashcat -m 22000 -a 0 home_wifi.hc22000 \
  /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt \
  -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule \
  --session=wifi_audit -w 3 --status --status-timer=15
```

`--session=wifi_audit` so this can be safely interrupted and resumed; `-w 3` pushes throughput since this machine isn't being used for anything else during the run; `--status` gives progress checkpoints instead of a silent screen.

## 5. If that fails, try a mask based on a known router-default pattern

Say the router's sticker showed an 8-digit-only default that was since changed, but you suspect a similar habit:

```bash
hashcat -m 22000 -a 3 home_wifi.hc22000 --increment \
  --increment-min=8 --increment-max=10 ?d?d?d?d?d?d?d?d?d?d
```

`--increment` tries lengths 8 through 10 rather than committing to exactly 10 digits.

## 6. Show the result

```bash
hashcat -m 22000 --show home_wifi.hc22000
```

## Part B: forgotten ZIP password

## 7. Extract the hash

```bash
zip2john old_backup.zip > /tmp/zip.hash
```

## 8. Crack it, chaining a rule attack then a loopback extension

```bash
hashcat -m 13600 -a 0 /tmp/zip.hash \
  /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt \
  -r /usr/share/hashcat/rules/best64.rule --loopback
```

`--loopback` means if the rule attack cracks something, hashcat automatically tries that newly-found password (as-is) against any other remaining hashes too — useful when a backup archive has multiple password-protected entries that might share a password.

## 9. Show, and clean up the session

```bash
hashcat -m 13600 --show /tmp/zip.hash
rm /tmp/zip.hash
```

## What this walkthrough covered

`-I`, `-b`, `--identify`, straight and mask attack modes (`-a 0`/`-a 3`), `-r` rules, `--increment`, `--session`/`--status`, `-w` workload tuning, `--loopback`, `--show`, and the standard extract-then-crack hand-off pattern from a companion tool (`zip2john`) into hashcat.
